Mindl Cohen joins us on The Shmooze to talk about the "2019 Pakn Treger Digital Translation Issue," a collection of letters and stories about letters. The pieces included in this year's anthology provide a window into the personal lives of Yiddish writers; illustrate aspects of day-to-day communications; and remind readers of the great distances across which relationships can stretch. A map of the word orl ערל 'non-Jew' based on the LCAAJ data. This map has two significant improvements over the previous ones. First, this is made with the new base map which has almost all of the location names added so that one can more easily identify where Jews said what. Second, I've left only the borders of the major dialects in color, the rest is colorless — so as not to interfere with the colors of the dots. (In the previous maps, a yellow dot in the blue Northeastern area would appear greenish, for example.) Another minor improvement is the occasional use of another symbol (a triangle) to indicate a particular variation: vocalization of final /l/ to /u/ (presumably by way of /ɫ/) as in /uru/. 

The word orl ערל has three main variants depending on the main vowel: O, U, or E. The standard form /orl/ (in green) is used only in Northeastern and to a some extent in Western, where the vowel is often lengthened by the following /r/. Central and Southeastern are dominated by U-forms (in pink/purple), also often with vowel lengthening. Central is notable for its many sorts of /l/; there is the velarized or dark /ɫ/ familiar from Polish; a palatalized /ʎ/; a syllablic /l̩/; and a voicless fricative /ɬ/ apparently pronunced like this:

https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ea/Voiceless_alveolar_lateral_fricative.ogg

Not much can be said about Southeastern because, for whatever reason, the data does not appear in the answer sheets. Perhaps the word was not used much in the Ukraine?

Most interesting are the E-forms which appear in every dialect, especially in the northern Northeasrn and in western Western (e.g., Alsace is all E). The simplest explanation is that /erl/ is a spelling pronunciation, since the word is spelled with an ayin — but that is unconvincing because Jews as a collective did not make such "m

Boite de 10 x 7 x 2 cm contenant des matrices yiddish, police de 10 points, pour une presse linotype. L'objet, ayant appartenu à Perets Guterman, a été offert à la Maison de la culture yiddish par sa nièce, Berthe Burko-Falcman, que nous remercions vivement.
Perets Guterman (1901-1980) a été journaliste, rédacteur et typographe. Né à Radom (Pologne), il a vécu à Lodz, puis à Varsovie (1919-1939) où il a travaillé en tant que typographe pour le journal bundiste Folkstsaytung. Au début de la Deuxième Guerre mondiale, il s'est enfui en URSS où il a été emprisonné dans le Goulag. Libéré en 1941, il est parti à Boukara, où il a travaillé pour l’ambassade polonaise. En 1942, il a quitté l’URSS avec l’armée polonaise, en passant par l’Iran et la Palestine. À partir de 1946, il a vécu en France. Il écrivait des chroniques, reportages et articles polémiques pour la presse bundiste à New York et à Paris. Pendant plusieurs années, il a été rédacteur du journal Undzer shtime (Paris), pour lequel il a également travaillé comme typographe. Il est mort à Paris le 11 mai 1980.
Ce document fait partie de « Passages : la vie culturelle yiddish en France », projet de documentation et de numérisation de la Maison de la culture yiddish – Bibliothèque Medem : www.cultureyiddish.com.

transcription: Rita Sorel Newborn - 1926-2017 - whose recordings are archived also - was a professional lyric and coloratura soprano, crossing over from classical to popular repertoire.  Born in Brooklyn, she had her own program in 1947 on the vastly popular Yiddish language station in New York, WEVD-NY.  She married Captain Solomon Newborn - whose letters home are also archived from WWII - and moved from NYC to the Long Island suburbs (Plainview), purchasing a small tract home in 1953 via the GI Bill.  She continued singing especially at major Long Island political and national events - such as the dedication of Sagamore Hill in Oyster Bay, Teddy Rooseveltt's summer White Rose as a National Park. Later she worked as an actress, appearing on request of Woody Allen and in other films as a SAG member, along with SNL -Saturday Night Live, in commercials, etc. http://www.judnewborn.com

Who would have thought that Jews being held in a "death camp" would be allowed to write postcards to the outside?  Yet that is what we seem to have here.

I haven't been able to get a complete translation through this style of script yet.  If anyone more proficient can help with this, please leave your translation in the "comments" area below.  

One thing that seems to jump out, as it were, is the comment penciled on the front that mentions of death in the camp are censored.  Then I can read full well that a death is mentioned in the postcard!  A case of "proof by assumption"?  Much of it looks like usual post card chit chat.  Very interesting though, that Hitler's "City for the Jews" really did have them writing back home.

"My card and --- greetings to you."  "Away --- I think it is very (barge) here after (since?) Erich is continuing to work in the ---."  "Christa is having her birthday in the Church." "Please think about me often and write."  "Daddy is in (building?) 15/70." "At the war area (?) beloved Langean (?) has died." "Here Rossleg Street #1 ---- is very --- after Erich let nearly  ---- from --- loose."   "December 5, 1943"
